summary: A struct groups values of different types under one name, with each member in its own storage. A union overlays its members in the same storage so only one is meaningful at a time. An enum names a set of integer constants. Together they let you model records, variants, and states.

sections.heading: Structures
sections.body: Define a struct type, create variables, and access members with `.` (or `->` through a pointer). Initialize with a list or designated initializers; uninitialized automatic members hold garbage.

sections.heading: typedef, nesting, and self-reference
bullets: `typedef struct {...} Student;` removes the need to write `struct` each time.
A struct can hold a pointer to its own type, which is how linked lists and trees are built.
Struct assignment copies all members (a shallow copy: pointers are copied, not what they point to).
sections.code: typedef struct Node { int val; struct Node *next; } Node;

sections.heading: Passing and returning structs
sections.body: Structs are passed by value, copying every byte, so pass a `const struct *` for large ones. Returning small structs by value is fine and common.

sections.heading: Unions
sections.body: All members share one block whose size is the size of the largest member (plus any alignment padding). Writing one member overwrites the others. Reading a different member than was last written reinterprets the bytes (allowed for type punning in C, implementation-defined result).

sections.heading: Enumerations
sections.body: An enum defines named integer constants starting at 0 unless assigned. Use them in place of magic numbers, especially for states and error codes.
sections.code:
enum State { IDLE, RUNNING = 5, STOPPED };   // 0, 5, 6
enum State st = RUNNING;

sections.body: Pair a union with an enum tag that records which member is active, and switch on the tag before reading. This is how interpreters, protocol parsers, and many C APIs represent 'one of several types'.
sections.code:
struct Val { enum { INT, FLT } kind; union { int i; float f; } u; };
void print(struct Val v) { if (v.kind == INT) printf("%d", v.u.i); else printf("%f", v.u.f); }

bullets: Struct: size is at least the sum of members (plus padding); all members valid at once.
Union: size is the largest member; only one valid at once.
Both can be nested in each other.
Anonymous unions (C11) expose members without a union name.

sections.body: A struct may end with an array of unspecified length, allocated together with its header, as used for packets and strings with a length prefix.

`unsigned ready : 1;` allocates one bit. Layout and ordering are implementation-defined, so bit-fields are fine for compact in-memory flags but unreliable for wire formats or hardware registers across compilers.

Copying a struct that contains a `char *name` duplicates only the pointer, so both copies refer to the same string and freeing one invalidates the other. Write a clone function that allocates and copies pointed-to data when you need independence.

takeaways: Struct members have separate storage; union members overlap.
Use . for values and -> for pointers; pass big structs by const pointer.
Combine a union with an enum tag to build safe variants.
Struct copy is shallow; layout and padding follow alignment rules.

references.label: Kernighan & Ritchie, The C Programming Language, 2nd ed.
